slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Begin by naming the appendix as a pivot rather than an afterthought. The course has already compared Euclidean and hyperbolic behavior through the parallel problem; Appendix A asks what happens when the visible symptom changes again. The lecture follows five objects: sphere, antipodal quotient, curvature, metric, and geodesic.

slides.title: Parallel Trichotomy
slides.notes: Use this slide to recover the course narrative before adding new machinery. Euclidean geometry gives one parallel, hyperbolic geometry gives many, and elliptic geometry removes parallels in the plane. The important transition is that a changed parallel statement demands a changed model language, not just a different drawing style.

slides.title: Sphere Before Quotient
slides.notes: Present the sphere as an excellent first model and also as an incomplete one. Great circles are convincing line candidates because they are symmetric and locally shortest. Yet two distinct great circles meet at two antipodal points, so a plane incidence axiom expecting one intersection has not been modeled cleanly yet.

slides.title: Antipodal Identification
slides.notes: The quotient operation is the central construction in the elliptic part of the appendix. Stress that it is not a visual trick. It changes what counts as a point, so the two antipodal meetings of great circles become a single elliptic meeting. That repair also changes separation and sidedness.

slides.title: Separation Replaces Between
slides.notes: This is the most syntactic slide in the elliptic sequence. The aim is not to list every separation axiom, but to explain why the axioms are needed. Once a line is circular and antipodal points are identified, ordinary between-language no longer has the same meaning, so separation becomes the replacement relation.

slides.title: Segments and Triangles
slides.notes: Here the lecture should slow down and separate representation from definition. A spherical drawing chooses representatives, but the elliptic object is an equivalence class under antipodal identification. That distinction prevents students from trusting a single sketch too much when defining segments, triangles, or sides of a line.

slides.title: Elliptic Plane Inventory
slides.notes: The table is meant to prevent a common misconception: elliptic geometry is not just spherical geometry drawn on a ball. It is a quotient model with altered global logic. The finite diameter is especially worth emphasizing, because finiteness here does not mean an edge where the geometry stops.

slides.title: Higher-Dimensional Surprise
slides.notes: Keep this slide conceptual. The point is not to develop elliptic three-space in full, but to show students that the word parallel can mutate when dimension and model change. A plane theorem about intersecting lines does not forbid higher-dimensional equidistant line families, so the vocabulary must track the setting.

slides.title: Riemannian Pivot
slides.notes: This slide marks the transition from elliptic geometry to Riemannian geometry. The key phrase is local measurement. Instead of first asking how many parallels exist, Riemannian geometry equips each tangent plane with a measuring rule and then derives distance, angle, curvature, and geodesic behavior from that rule.

slides.title: Curve Curvature
slides.notes: The appendix builds surface curvature by first recalling curve curvature. Make the osculating circle tactile: it is the circle that best matches position and tangent direction at the point. A smaller radius means tighter bending. Signed curvature then records which side of the tangent line the bending occupies.

slides.title: Surface Curvature
slides.notes: Connect this slide to the previous one by saying that a surface can be sliced by many planes through the normal line. Each slice gives an ordinary curve curvature. The principal curvatures are the extreme values, and their product is Gaussian curvature. The sign examples should be read before the formula is trusted.

slides.title: Intrinsic Curvature
slides.notes: Use the cylinder to explain the intrinsic point gently. Students may think all visible bending counts as curvature. The cylinder bends extrinsically, but its Gaussian curvature is zero because the surface can be unrolled without changing internal distances. That prepares the meaning of Gauss's remarkable theorem.

slides.title: Metric Tensor
slides.notes: Translate the metric formula into a measuring device. The expression for ds squared tells the surface how to convert small coordinate changes into length. The ellipses make this visible: they are what the metric considers unit vectors at different points, so varying ellipses mean varying local geometry.

slides.title: Riemann Generalization
slides.notes: This slide should feel like a conceptual widening. Riemann's innovation was not simply a new surface example; it was the abstraction of geometry into a smoothly varying quadratic form in any dimension. Once that rule is available, curvature can be encoded by tensors and summarized in several useful ways.

slides.title: Geodesics
slides.notes: Return to the word line, but now through the Riemannian lens. A geodesic generalizes straightness by asking the metric for locally shortest or zero geodesic curvature paths. Use the great circle and cylinder helix to separate local straightness from global shortest distance.

slides.title: Unifying Map
slides.notes: This synthesis slide supplies the lecture thesis explicitly. The appendix starts from a familiar course question about parallels, but it ends by suggesting that parallelism is only one observable feature. The deeper objects are model choice, topology, metric, curvature, and geodesics, which together organize modern geometry.

slides.title: Teaching Lab
slides.notes: End with an activity that forces translation. Students should not simply repeat that elliptic geometry has no parallels. They should take a familiar claim, state what the model's points and lines are, decide whether a metric is needed, and then identify the exact place where the old Euclidean proof changes.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the course arc. Appendix A adds a compact preview of modern differential geometry while staying tied to the original parallel problem. The final habit is diagnostic: when a claim changes, locate the changed structure. That habit will keep elliptic geometry and Riemannian geometry from feeling like disconnected topics.
